section.title: The Lame Beggar Healed
section.sectionRationale: The Spirit-filled church now bears public witness. Peter and John, going up to the temple, heal a man lame from birth in the name of Jesus. The astonished crowd gathers, and Peter seizes the moment to preach: the power is not their own but comes through faith in the risen Jesus, the Servant, the Author of life, whom they crucified and God raised. He calls them to repent and points to Jesus as the prophet Moses foretold and the offspring in whom all nations are blessed.
section.thesis: In the name of the crucified and risen Jesus, the Author of life, a man lame from birth is made whole, and Peter turns the wonder into a summons to repent and turn to the Servant God raised up, the prophet Moses promised, through whom the blessing of Abraham reaches all the families of the earth.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the healing of the lame man in Jesus' name at the temple gate; Peter's charge that the crowd killed the Author of life whom God raised, and the faith in Jesus' name that healed the man; and the call to repent, with Jesus proclaimed as the promised prophet and the offspring of blessing.

units.label: Healed in the name of Jesus
units.note: in the name of Jesus Christ, get up and walk

verses.text: One afternoon Peter and John were going up to the temple at the hour of prayer, the ninth hour.
And a man who was lame from birth was being carried to the temple gate called Beautiful, where he was put every day to beg from those entering the temple courts.
When he saw Peter and John about to enter, he asked them for money.
Peter looked directly at him, as did John. “Look at us!” said Peter.
So the man gave them his attention, expecting to receive something from them.
But Peter said, “Silver or gold I do not have, but what I have I give you: In the {{onoma|name}} of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, get up and walk!”
Taking him by the right hand, Peter helped him up, and at once the man’s feet and ankles were made strong.
He sprang to his feet and began to walk. Then he went with them into the temple courts, walking and leaping and praising God.
When all the people saw him walking and praising God,
they recognized him as the man who used to sit begging at the Beautiful Gate of the temple, and they were filled with wonder and amazement at what had happened to him.

units.label: You killed the Author of life, but God raised Him
units.note: faith in the name of Jesus made him strong

verses.text: While the man clung to Peter and John, all the people were astonished and ran to them in the walkway called Solomon’s Colonnade.
And when Peter saw this, he addressed the people: “Men of Israel, why are you surprised by this? Why do you stare at us as if by our own power or godliness we had made this man walk?
The God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the God of our fathers, has glorified His {{pais|servant}} Jesus. You handed Him over and rejected Him before Pilate, even though he had decided to release Him.
You rejected the Holy and Righteous One and asked that a murderer be released to you.
You killed the {{archegos|Author}} of life, but God raised Him from the dead, and we are witnesses of this fact.
By faith in the name of Jesus, this man whom you see and know has been made strong. It is Jesus’ name and the faith that comes through Him that has given him this complete healing in your presence.

units.label: Repent and turn: the promised prophet and the blessing of the nations
units.note: times of refreshing and the restoration of all things

verses.text: And now, brothers, I know that you acted in ignorance, as did your leaders.
But in this way God has fulfilled what He foretold through all the prophets, saying that His Christ would suffer.
Repent, then, and turn back, so that your sins may be wiped away,
that times of refreshing may come from the presence of the Lord, and that He may send Jesus, the Christ, who has been appointed for you.
Heaven must take Him in until the time comes for the {{apokatastasis|restoration}} of all things, which God announced long ago through His holy prophets.
For Moses said, ‘The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers. You must listen to Him in everything He tells you.
Everyone who does not listen to Him will be completely cut off from among his people.’
Indeed, all the prophets from Samuel on, as many as have spoken, have proclaimed these days.
And you are sons of the prophets and of the covenant God made with your fathers when He said to Abraham, ‘Through your offspring all the families of the earth will be blessed.’
When God raised up His Servant, He sent Him first to you to bless you by turning each of you from your wicked ways.”

onoma.gloss: Name, and by extension the authority and person named. Peter heals not by his own power but in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth. Throughout Acts the name of Jesus carries His saving authority; it is by faith in that name that the lame man is made whole.

pais.gloss: Servant, or child. Peter calls Jesus God's servant, echoing the suffering Servant of Isaiah whom God glorifies. The title binds the healing and the sermon to the prophecies of the one who would suffer for the people and then be exalted.

archegos.gloss: Author, originator, pioneer, prince. Peter charges that they killed the Author of life, the very source of life, yet God raised Him. The irony is sharp: they put to death the one from whom all life flows, and He now gives strength to a lame man.

apokatastasis.gloss: Restoration, setting all things right again. Heaven receives Jesus until the time of the restoration of all things that God promised through the prophets. It looks to the renewal of creation at Christ's return, the final undoing of the ruin of the fall.

basic.context: After Pentecost, the Spirit-filled church begins to bear public witness. Peter and John go up to the temple at the afternoon hour of prayer. A man lame from birth, who begs daily at the gate called Beautiful, asks them for money. Peter has no silver or gold, but in the name of Jesus he commands the man to walk, and he is instantly healed. The crowd runs together in amazement, and Peter preaches, turning their attention from himself to the risen Jesus and calling them to repent.
basic.hermeneutics: Read the healing as a sign that opens a sermon. The questions to ask are: by whose power was the man healed, what does Peter say the crowd did to Jesus and what God did in response, and what does Peter call them to do? Notice how the miracle is never the point in itself; it is a signpost to the risen Christ and an occasion to call for repentance.
basic.originalLanguages: The man is healed in the onoma, the name, of Jesus, that is, by His authority. Peter calls Jesus God's pais, His Servant, echoing Isaiah, and the archegos, the Author of life, whom they killed and God raised. He points forward to the apokatastasis, the restoration of all things, when Christ returns to make all things new.
basic.typology: Jesus is the prophet like Moses whom God promised to raise up, to whom the people must listen. He is the Servant of Isaiah, glorified through suffering. He is the offspring of Abraham through whom all the families of the earth are blessed. The healed man, leaping and praising God, pictures the restoration the gospel brings.
basic.christ: Peter's message is dense with titles for Jesus: God's Servant, the Holy and Righteous One, the Author of life, the Christ who had to suffer, the prophet like Moses, the offspring of blessing. He was rejected and killed but raised by God, and it is by faith in His name that the man is healed. Christ is the source of both the healing and the salvation Peter offers.
basic.god: The God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the God of the fathers, has glorified His Servant Jesus. God fulfilled through the suffering of Christ what He foretold through all the prophets. God raised Jesus and will send Him again at the restoration of all things. Everything is God's doing, keeping His ancient covenant promises.
basic.crossReferences: Deuteronomy 18 is the promise of a prophet like Moses that Peter applies to Jesus. Genesis 22 is the promise that Abraham's offspring would bless all nations. Isaiah 52 and 53 stand behind the title of the suffering Servant. Acts 4 continues the story as the healing leads to opposition and bold testimony.
basic.oneStory: The risen Christ, now reigning, heals through His name and sends His witnesses to call Israel to repentance. Peter shows that Jesus is the fulfillment of everything the prophets promised, from Moses to Abraham, and that in Him the blessing of the nations and the restoration of all things have begun. The gospel that started in Jerusalem is on its way to the ends of the earth.

context.literary:
Luke builds the chapter as a diptych with a hinge. The first panel, verses 1 to 10, is told almost like a film: three movements of the man's body, carried, held, then springing up, and three verbs of his joy, 'walking and leaping and praising God.' The hinge is verse 11, where a clinging man and a running crowd draw everyone toward the apostles. The second panel, verses 12 to 26, is Peter's speech, and it begins with the very question the crowd is asking, 'why are you surprised by this?'

The sermon is shaped as a movement from the past to the future. Verses 12 to 16 look back to what was done to Jesus, with a series of sharp contrasts between what the people did and what God did: 'You handed Him over... God has glorified His servant'; 'You killed the Author of life, but God raised Him.' Verses 17 and 18 turn on the word 'And now,' where excuse and fulfilment meet. Verses 19 to 21 look forward to repentance, refreshing and the restoration of all things. Verses 22 to 26 close by gathering the Scriptures, Moses, Samuel and all the prophets, Abraham, so that the sermon ends where Israel's story began.

The passage also lines up with the Pentecost sermon and with the Gospel. Both speeches in Acts 2 and 3 move from event to Scripture to the cross and resurrection to repentance. The healing itself has parallels with Luke's earlier stories: a blind beggar who followed Jesus 'glorifying God' while all the people gave praise, Luke 18:43, and a paralytic who stood up and went home 'glorifying God,' Luke 5:25. Luke writes the first miracle of the apostles in the same shape as the miracles of the Master, so the reader sees that the works of Jesus continue through His name.
context.historical:
The ninth hour, three in the afternoon, was the time of the evening offering. The law required a lamb at twilight each day, Exodus 29:39 and 41, and prayer in the temple was tied to that hour, as when Daniel was visited 'about the time of the evening sacrifice,' Daniel 9:21. Peter and John, still devout Jews who attended the temple, are doing what pious people did. Luke never suggests that the church had yet left the temple behind.

The Beautiful Gate cannot be located with certainty. Many scholars place it on the east side of the court and some identify it with a large bronze gate, but the ancient sources do not settle it, and Luke does not need us to know. What matters is that it stood at a threshold where worshippers passed in numbers, which made it a standard place for a beggar. Charity at the temple was an act of merit, and a man laid there every day relied on the pious in the moment of going in to God.

His condition mattered in another way. The law barred priests with a defect from approaching the altar, and 'lame' is on the list, Leviticus 21:18. A saying from the days of David was still repeated, 'The blind and the lame will never enter the palace,' 2 Samuel 5:8. The man could be carried to the gate, but he was on the wrong side of a long line of exclusion. When he walks into the court, a barrier is crossed.

Solomon's Colonnade ran along the eastern side of the temple court. It was a roofed walkway where crowds could gather and teachers could speak, and it is where Jesus Himself had walked in the Feast of Dedication, John 10:23. Peter speaks in the same place. The addressees are 'Men of Israel,' a temple crowd, many of whom had been in the city when Jesus was tried. The charge that they 'handed Him over' before Pilate is rooted in the trial narratives, Luke 23:13 to 25.
context.canonical:
The chapter is a tapestry of Old Testament hopes, each of which Peter names or recalls. Isaiah 35:6 said that in the age of salvation 'the lame will leap like a deer,' and the Greek Old Testament uses the verb for leaping that Luke uses of the healed man in verse 8. Isaiah 52:13 spoke of the Servant who would be 'raised and lifted up and highly exalted,' and Peter's 'God has glorified His servant Jesus' in verse 13 draws on that line. Moses promised a prophet like himself, Deuteronomy 18:15 to 19, which Peter quotes. Genesis 22:18 promised that through Abraham's offspring all nations of the earth would be blessed, and Peter quotes it in verse 25.

Peter also reads Israel's story as one long preparation. He says that God 'foretold through all the prophets' that His Christ would suffer, verse 18, a claim that Jesus Himself made on the road to Emmaus, Luke 24:25 to 27, and again to the eleven, Luke 24:44 to 46. He says that all the prophets 'from Samuel on' pointed to these days, verse 24. And he says that heaven holds Jesus until the 'restoration of all things,' verse 21, language that echoes the question the disciples put in Acts 1:6 and Jesus' own saying that Elijah would come and restore all things, Matthew 17:11.

The passage is also picked up elsewhere. Stephen cites the same prophet like Moses in Acts 7:37. Paul reads the promise to Abraham as good news for the Gentiles, Galatians 3:8, and as pointing to one offspring, Christ, Galatians 3:16. Hebrews calls Jesus 'the author of their salvation,' Hebrews 2:10, using the same noun as Peter's 'Author of life.' And the 'name' of Jesus, which heals the man here, becomes the only name for salvation in Acts 4:12.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Luke gives this miracle and sermon to show that the risen Christ is still at work in the world through the name by which He is invoked, and that the church's first act of power is a work of mercy that ends in preaching. The first half of the chapter shows the gospel arriving in the body of a man who has been excluded from Israel's worship; the second half names what the healing means. Peter takes care to say that the apostles themselves have not done it, 'by our own power or godliness,' verse 12, so that all glory runs to Jesus.

Luke also means to answer a question the Jewish reader would be asking: if Jesus is the Messiah, why did Israel's leaders put Him to death? The answer given here is both honest and merciful. The people did act, and they are told so plainly. But they acted in ignorance, and God used even this to fulfil what the prophets foretold, so the door to repentance stands open. The aim of the speech is not to condemn but to call.

Finally, Luke wants the reader to see that the Servant, the prophet like Moses and the offspring of Abraham are one person, and that the blessing promised to the nations begins at Jerusalem, 'first to you,' verse 26. The blessing is defined as being turned from wickedness, so that Israel's repentance is not a side issue but the first form of the world's blessing.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The details of the miracle belong to a particular scene. The apostles say 'Silver or gold I do not have,' verse 6, and then give the healing; nothing in the text gives believers a formula to repeat, and the gesture of the right hand is not a rite. In the same way, the way Peter handles the crowd is a narrative of how he spoke to that audience on that day, not a script for all preaching.

What is prescriptive lies in what Peter commands and what the passage teaches by implication. 'Repent, then, and turn back,' verse 19, is addressed to every hearer, and the promised results, sins wiped away, refreshing from the Lord's presence, are promises to anyone who turns. Acts also shows the attitude of the apostles: they give what they have, they refuse credit, and they turn every sign into a call to Jesus. Those habits belong to every believer. A reader should also notice what the apostles do not do. They do not promise health to the crowd, and they do not make healing the main message. The man's walking is a sign pointing to a larger restoration which will come when 'the restoration of all things' arrives, verse 21.

debates.question: Does the healing of the lame man show that physical healing in Jesus' name is guaranteed for believers today?

views.label: A sign authenticating the apostolic message
views.case: The wonders and signs in Acts confirm the apostles as authorized witnesses of the risen Christ, Acts 2:43 and Hebrews 2:3-4. The healing serves the preaching of the gospel and points to Jesus; it is descriptive of that founding era, not a blanket promise of healing on demand for every Christian.

views.label: A pattern of the kingdom's healing power still available
views.case: Others hold that the same risen Christ still heals through His people, that the name of Jesus retains its power, and that believers should expect and pray for healing as an ongoing expression of the kingdom breaking in, while leaving the outcome to God.

debates.bearing: Both agree the healing points beyond itself to the risen Christ and the salvation offered in His name; the deeper wholeness Peter presses toward is repentance, forgiveness, and the restoration of all things, which no one should reduce to bodily healing alone.

debates.question: What does Peter mean when he says Israel acted 'in ignorance,' and does that excuse them?

views.label: A genuine mitigation that opens the way to repentance
views.case: The law distinguished between sins done unintentionally, for which atonement was provided, and sins done defiantly, for which there was none, Numbers 15:27 to 31. Jesus prayed on the cross, 'Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing,' Luke 23:34, and Paul says he received mercy because he 'acted in ignorance and unbelief,' 1 Timothy 1:13. Peter is placing the nation under the first category so that forgiveness can be offered.

views.label: An explanation, not an excuse
views.case: Peter has just said that they handed over, rejected and killed the Author of life, and he tells them to repent so that their sins may be wiped away. The ignorance does not remove guilt; it describes why the guilt could be forgiven. Stephen later says that the people always resist the Holy Spirit, Acts 7:51, which suggests the ignorance was culpable.

debates.bearing: Both views agree that the call to repent stands, and that ignorance is not innocence. Luke holds firmly to guilt and to mercy at once, and the ignorance defines the people's situation without taking away their need to turn.

debates.question: When do 'times of refreshing' and 'the restoration of all things' arrive?

views.label: Both belong to the age begun with Christ's resurrection
views.case: Peter links the refreshing to repentance now, 'so that your sins may be wiped away, that times of refreshing may come,' verses 19 and 20, and Acts 2 has shown the Spirit already poured out. The restoration then begins with Christ's reign and is completed when He returns, so that the present is the first fruit of the whole.

views.label: Both wait for the return of Christ
views.case: Others read the refreshing and the restoration as a single future event tied to the sending of Jesus, 'the Christ, who has been appointed for you,' verse 20, and the heaven that 'must take Him in until the time comes,' verse 21. On this reading the repentance of Israel is a condition for the coming of the final day.

debates.bearing: The text does not fix the timetable. What it does fix is the link between turning to Christ and the hope of His coming, and the assurance that the restoration God announced long ago will come as certainly as the healing of this man.

study.originalLanguages:
The man was 'lame from birth,' literally lame from his mother's womb, and Luke calls him by the common Greek word cholos, which is also the word of the Greek Old Testament in Isaiah 35:6, where 'the lame will leap like a deer.' The verb used of his springing up, hallomai, in verse 8 is the same verb that Isaiah's translators chose for the leap. The man does exactly what the prophet said the lame would do, and Luke says it twice, once with 'leaping' and once with 'praising.'

Peter's command is 'get up and walk,' verse 6. The verb for 'get up,' egeiro, is the verb of resurrection. Luke uses it when Peter takes the man's right hand and 'raised' him up, verse 7, and again when Peter says that God 'raised' Jesus from the dead, verse 15. Elsewhere Luke uses anistemi, 'raise up,' as in verses 22 and 26. The same family of words runs through the chapter and joins the healed man to the risen Lord.

Verse 15 gives Jesus a title, archegos, 'Author of life.' The word is built from archo, 'to begin or lead,' and means founder, leader or pioneer. It appears again at Acts 5:31, where Jesus is 'Prince' and Savior, and in Hebrews 2:10 and 12:2, where He is the 'author' and 'perfecter' of faith. Here it sits in grim irony beside the verb for the crowd's act, 'You killed,' and beside their request that a murderer be 'granted' to them, verse 14, where the Greek verb charizomai means to give as a favor. The people asked for the life of a killer as a gift and put to death the giver of life.

Peter says the man has been given 'complete healing,' verse 16. The noun holokleria means soundness in every part, from the adjective that Paul uses of a spirit, soul and body kept whole in 1 Thessalonians 5:23. Peter does not ask for a limb to be repaired but for the whole man to be set right, and so the physical wholeness stands for the greater sense in which sins are wiped away.

Verse 19 asks for two actions, 'Repent, and turn back.' The first, metanoeo, is a change of mind; the second, epistrepho, is to turn around, the word used for a return to God. The result is that sins may be 'wiped away,' from exaleipho, which means to wipe out, to blot out writing. David prays 'blot out my transgressions' in Psalm 51:1, and the same family of words describes a debt cancelled. Then 'times of refreshing' come, from anapsyxis, a breathing space or revival related to a verb for cooling and drawing breath, the relief of a weary traveller who finds shade.

In verse 21 the 'restoration of all things' is apokatastasis. It is the noun of the verb that the disciples used in Acts 1:6 when they asked if Jesus would 'restore' the kingdom to Israel, and of the verb Jesus uses of Elijah in Matthew 17:11. And the repeated 'must,' dei, in verse 21 marks a divine necessity: heaven must receive Him, as Luke 24:26 had said the Christ must suffer. Finally, in verse 26 the Servant is God's pais, a word that may mean servant or child, and Luke uses it of Jesus here, in verse 13 and in Acts 4:27 and 30.

typology.fulfillment: Isaiah described the age of salvation as one in which the eyes of the blind are opened and 'the lame will leap like a deer.' The healed man at the Beautiful Gate leaps and praises God, and Jesus Himself pointed to such healings as the sign that the age had begun, Luke 7:22. The escalation is that the miracle is not merely an event but a sample of the coming restoration, and Peter immediately speaks of 'the restoration of all things,' verse 21. The type falls short in one respect. The man will still die, and the full removal of infirmity awaits the resurrection, Revelation 21:4.

Moses promised that the LORD would raise up a prophet like him, to be heard in everything, and that anyone who refused would be held accountable. Peter says that Jesus is that prophet, verse 22, and warns of being 'cut off' for refusing to listen, verse 23. Stephen says the same in Acts 7:37. The correspondence includes a rejected deliverer, signs and wonders, and a mediator of the word of God. The escalation is that Jesus is more than a mediator: He is the Author of life and the One who sits at the right hand of God. Moses was faithful as a servant, Hebrews 3:5, but Jesus is the Son.

Isaiah's Servant would be 'raised and lifted up and highly exalted,' and Peter says 'God has glorified His servant Jesus,' verse 13, after setting the glory beside the handing over and the rejection. The Servant song goes on to say that He was crushed and made a guilt offering, Isaiah 53:10, and Peter says that this suffering was foretold, verse 18. The escalation is that the suffering and the glory belong to one person. The type is not a picture of a king in the old sense, but a description of a person, and Jesus fulfils it in His own life, death, and resurrection.

God swore that through Abraham's offspring all nations of the earth would be blessed. Peter says that the people are 'sons of the prophets and of the covenant,' verse 25, and that God sent His Servant to them first. Paul argues that the singular 'offspring' means one person, Christ, Galatians 3:16. The correspondence is that a promise made to one man blesses many nations. The escalation is that the blessing is defined: it is to be turned from one's wicked ways, verse 26. The type has not yet reached its end, since the blessing of the nations is still spreading, but it has begun at Jerusalem.

study.christ:
Peter's sermon gives Jesus a cluster of titles, and every one of them is drawn from the Scriptures. He is God's 'servant,' pais, verses 13 and 26, the figure of Isaiah 52 and 53 who suffers and is exalted. He is 'the Holy and Righteous One,' verse 14, a pair of titles that no earthly accused ought to bear and that no earthly judge ought to have rejected. He is 'the Author of life,' verse 15, the one who gives life and leads the way to it. He is the 'Christ' who suffers, verse 18, and the 'Christ' who will be sent again, verse 20. He is the prophet like Moses who must be heard, verse 22, and the offspring of Abraham through whom the nations are blessed, verse 25.

Together these titles show that Israel's Scriptures hold one person in view from several angles. Moses sees the prophet, Abraham the offspring, Isaiah the servant, and the psalms the anointed one. The shared claim is that suffering was no accident. Jesus told the disciples on the road to Emmaus that the Christ had to suffer and then enter His glory, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, Luke 24:25 to 27, and Peter now says the same.

The pattern of the chapter is one of reversal. The people 'handed Him over,' and God 'glorified' Him. They 'rejected' the Holy and Righteous One and asked for a murderer, and God raised the Author of life. Pilate had 'decided to release Him,' verse 13, a detail that matches Luke 23:13 to 25, so the guilt is not reduced to a misunderstanding but the mercy still reaches the guilty. At the centre of the reversal stands the name: 'by faith in the name of Jesus, this man whom you see and know has been made strong,' verse 16. The power of the name is the power of the person, who lives.

The chapter also puts Christ at the head of the future. 'Heaven must take Him in until the time comes for the restoration of all things,' verse 21. The ascended Christ is not absent but waiting, appointed, and sure to be sent. Thus Peter holds the cross behind him, the throne above him and the return before him, and he asks the crowd to see themselves between the first and the last.

A word of caution keeps this honest. The lame man is not a hidden portrait of Israel or of fallen humanity, and the gate called Beautiful is not a symbol of Christ. Luke gives them as persons and places. The links to Christ rest on what Peter says and on the Old Testament texts he cites. The healing is a sign, and the sign points to a Servant, a name and a promise that the apostles themselves explain.
study.god:
The God of this chapter is introduced with a name that grounds everything in the past: 'The God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the God of our fathers,' verse 13. The one who acts on the day is the same who made covenant with the patriarchs, and He keeps faith. The first thing Peter shows about God is continuity. The new thing is not a different God but the same God doing what He promised.

God is the one who glorifies. He lifts up the servant whom people rejected, verse 13, and He turns the shame of the cross into the road to glory. He is also the one who fulfils: 'God has fulfilled what He foretold through all the prophets,' verse 18. Even the actions of those who killed Jesus fall inside a purpose they did not understand. This does not remove their guilt, since Peter names it three times, but it shows a God whose plan does not fail even when people resist it.

He is a God of mercy that acts before it is asked. The man at the gate did not ask for healing; he asked for coins. Peter gives him something greater than he thought to desire. The same pattern appears in the call to repentance: God does not wait for a perfect response but supplies the offer, the means and the promise. He wipes away sins, sends refreshing, and promises to send Jesus. His own kindness is the ground of the appeal.

He is also a God whose presence is the source of refreshing. 'Times of refreshing may come from the presence of the Lord,' verse 20. The words recall the lost presence of Eden, and they promise that the presence that once drove people out will now draw them in. And He is a God of universal blessing, since the covenant He made with Abraham reaches 'all the families of the earth,' verse 25.

The chapter also holds together what might seem in tension. God is just, since He holds the people accountable for the cross and warns of being 'completely cut off,' verse 23. God is merciful, since He offers forgiveness to those same people. God is sovereign, since He ordained that the Christ should suffer, and humans are responsible, since they chose to reject Him. And God is both present and coming: He is at work through the name now, and He will send the Christ at the appointed time.

For worship, the man's response is the right one. He enters the temple he could never enter, 'walking and leaping and praising God.' The crowd's amazement turns to wonder and then to listening. The right response to a God who acts so freely is praise, and then a willingness to hear what He says through His chosen Prophet, to whom the people must listen 'in everything.'

crossReferences.note: Isaiah's picture of the age of salvation, when the blind see, the deaf hear, and the lame leap like a deer. The healed man's leaping at the Beautiful Gate is a small fulfilment of that promise, and it points to the larger restoration of all things which Peter announces in verse 21.

Jesus heals a paralytic who rises, takes up his mat and goes home glorifying God. The shape of the story is the same as the miracle at the gate, with the same command to rise, the same immediate standing and the same praise. Luke shows that the work of Jesus continues through His name in the hands of His witnesses.

A proverb from the capture of Jerusalem said that the blind and the lame would never enter the palace. The man at the gate belongs to a class barred from the house, and his walking into the court in praise shows how the name of Jesus overturns old exclusions.

Peter explains the same healing before the rulers, saying it was done by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom they crucified and God raised. The chapter picks up the miracle of chapter 3 and moves it from the temple crowd to the council, and from the healed man to the name by which all must be saved.

The promise of a prophet like Moses, with a warning for those who do not listen. Peter quotes it in verses 22 and 23 and applies it to Jesus. Stephen quotes the same text in Acts 7:37. It supplies the standard by which Israel must judge the One they have rejected.

The Servant is 'raised and lifted up and highly exalted.' Peter's statement that God has glorified His servant Jesus draws on this song, and the sermon then follows the song's own turn from suffering to glory, with the suffering foretold in verse 18.

After Abraham did not withhold his only son, God swore that through his offspring all nations of the earth would be blessed. Peter's quotation in verse 25 treats this as the root of the church's mission, and the way God provided His own Son for the world gives the promise its full weight.

The trial before Pilate, where he found Jesus not guilty and wanted to release Him, but the crowd demanded Barabbas, a man jailed for insurrection and murder. Peter's words in verses 13 and 14 about being 'handed over' and a murderer being requested are drawn directly from this scene.

The law's distinction between unintentional sin, which could be atoned for, and defiant sin, which could not. When Peter says that the people and their leaders acted in ignorance, verse 17, he places them in the category for which mercy is offered, and the call to repentance is an invitation to find it.

Jesus says that Elijah comes and will restore all things, using the verb behind Peter's noun in verse 21. The saying shows that the restoration is not the work of a human forerunner but the work of God's anointed, and Peter places it at the end of heaven's waiting.

Paul says that the Scripture foresaw God justifying the Gentiles by faith and told the gospel to Abraham in advance. This is the same promise that Peter quotes in verse 25, and Paul's reading shows how it moved from the sons of Israel to every nation.

Jesus is called the author of salvation, made perfect through suffering. The noun is the same as Peter's 'Author of life,' and the idea of the pioneer who goes first through suffering to glory is the heart of Peter's account of the cross and exaltation.

The setting for Peter's sermon is the same place where Jesus walked in the temple courts at the Feast of Dedication. The place that heard the Master's claims now hears His apostle's explanation, and a bold claim made there in winter is now seen in the light of the resurrection.

study.oneStory:
The chapter looks back to Eden by way of three promises. The man at the gate is a human being excluded from the worship of God, and the peoples of the earth have lived outside the garden since Genesis 3. The promise to Abraham in Genesis 12:3, that 'all the families of the earth will be blessed through you,' was God's answer to that exclusion, and Peter says the answer is now being delivered. The blessing is not an abstraction. It is the turning of each person from wickedness, verse 26.

It also looks back to the wilderness, where Moses mediated the word of God and the people drew back from the voice. Deuteronomy 18:16 recalls how they asked not to hear the LORD again at Horeb, and Moses promised a prophet who would stand in that place. Peter says the promised prophet has come and that to ignore Him is to be cut off. The question of who will listen, which runs through Israel's story, is now put to Jerusalem again.

What the chapter sets up is the conflict that follows. The preaching leads at once to arrest in Acts 4, and the name that heals becomes the name that divides. The message of Acts 3 is still gathering strength. Luke will take the word 'Servant' from Peter's lips into the church's prayer, Acts 4:27 and 30, and the claim that Jesus is the prophet like Moses into Stephen's speech and his death, Acts 7. The blessing of the nations, said to begin 'first' with Israel, moves outward, as Acts 8, 10 and 13 show, until Paul can say that the gospel foretold to Abraham has reached the Gentiles, Galatians 3:8.

The chapter also stretches forward to the end of the story. The restoration of all things is the work of the new creation: the lame leaping, the curse removed, and the presence of God again among His people. Revelation 21:4 describes the final state, with no more death, mourning, crying or pain. The healed man is a first sample. His walking is a small down payment on a restored creation, and the refreshing from the Lord's presence that Peter promises is the same presence that Revelation 22:4 says the redeemed will see face to face. In the meantime the church stands where Peter stood, between the Christ who has suffered and the Christ who will be sent, calling people to turn.

quiz.q: By what power did Peter heal the man lame from birth?

options.text: By the name of Jesus Christ, through faith in that name.
options.note: Peter is explicit: it is the name of Jesus and faith in Him, not his own power, that healed the man.

options.text: By speaking the name of Jesus over the man.
options.note: The name of Jesus is central, but Peter stresses that it is faith in that name, not a mere formula, that healed him.

options.text: By his own godliness and spiritual power.
options.note: Peter directly denies this, asking why they stare as if by their own power or godliness they made the man walk.

options.text: By the silver and gold he gave the beggar.
options.note: Peter had no silver or gold; he gave what he had, healing in Jesus' name.

quiz.q: What did Peter say the people had done to Jesus, and what did God do?

options.text: They killed the Author of life, but God raised Him from the dead.
options.note: Peter states the sharp contrast: they put to death the Author of life, and God raised Him.

options.text: They handed Jesus over to Pilate to be crucified.
options.note: True, Peter does say they handed Him over, but the striking heart of his charge is that they killed the Author of life whom God raised.

options.text: They misunderstood Jesus but were not really responsible.
options.note: Peter does say they acted in ignorance, yet he still holds them responsible for rejecting and killing Jesus.

options.text: They honored Jesus, and God rewarded them for it.
options.note: The opposite is true: they rejected and killed Him, though God raised Him and still offers them mercy.

quiz.q: What did Peter call the crowd to do in response?

options.text: Repent and turn back, so that their sins might be wiped away.
options.note: Peter's summons is to repent and turn to God for forgiveness.

options.text: Turn from their sins and stop doing wrong.
options.note: Repentance does mean turning from sin, but Peter's call is fuller: turn back to God so sins are wiped away and times of refreshing come.

options.text: Offer sacrifices at the temple to atone for killing Jesus.
options.note: Peter did not point them to temple sacrifice but to repentance and faith in the risen Christ.

options.text: Wait for a future prophet who would explain these things.
options.note: Peter says the promised prophet like Moses has already come in Jesus; the call is to listen to Him and repent now.

quiz.q: How does Peter present Jesus from the Old Testament?

options.text: As the suffering Servant, the prophet like Moses, and the offspring of Abraham who blesses all nations.
options.note: Peter draws these threads together to show Jesus fulfills the whole line of promise.

options.text: As the prophet like Moses whom the people must obey.
options.note: True and cited by Peter, but he also names Jesus the Servant and the offspring of Abraham, a fuller picture.

options.text: As a righteous teacher who kept the law of Moses.
options.note: Peter says far more than this: Jesus is the promised Servant, prophet, and offspring, raised from the dead.

options.text: As a political liberator who would free Israel from Rome.
options.note: Peter presents Jesus as the suffering and risen Christ, not a political deliverer.

quiz.q: What does the healing of the lame man point toward?

options.text: The risen Christ and the fuller restoration of all things He will bring.
options.note: The sign points beyond itself to the reigning Jesus and the coming restoration Peter proclaims.

options.text: The compassion of Peter and John for a poor beggar.
options.note: There is compassion here, but the point is not the apostles' kindness; it is a sign directing the crowd to Christ.

options.text: The power of the risen Jesus at work through His witnesses.
options.note: True and important, but the sign points further still, to the salvation and restoration found in Christ.

options.text: A reward given to the man for his years of faithful begging.
options.note: The healing was a free gift in Jesus' name, not a reward for the man's begging.

questions: Peter had no silver or gold, but he gave what he had in the name of Jesus. What has God given you that is worth more than money to share with someone in need?
The healed man went into the temple walking and leaping and praising God. What has Christ done in your life that makes you want to praise Him openly?
Peter refused to let the crowd credit him, pointing them instead to Jesus. When God works through you, how do you keep the attention on Christ rather than yourself?
Peter told the crowd they had acted in ignorance, yet still called them to repent. How does it comfort you that God meets even our worst failures with a call to turn back to Him?
Jesus is the prophet we must listen to in everything. Is there something Christ is saying to you through His word that you have been slow to obey?
God sent His risen Servant to bless people by turning them from their wicked ways. What would it mean to receive that blessing as a turning, not just a comfort, this week?

translationNotes.note: The ninth hour is explained in a footnote as three in the afternoon, one of the set times of prayer at the temple.
The word rendered servant carries a footnote reading or His child; the term echoes the suffering Servant of Isaiah whom God glorifies, and it recurs in verse 26.
Peter quotes Deuteronomy 18:15 and 18:19 about the prophet like Moses, applying the promise to Jesus.
The promise through your offspring all the families of the earth will be blessed is drawn from Genesis 22:18, the covenant with Abraham.
